title: Annotation-Efficient U-Net Enables High-Content Mitochondrial Morphometry in Widefield Fluorescence Images
content: Mitochondrial morphology is intrinsically linked to cellular stress and disease states, yet quantitative characterization across cell populations presents an inherent trade-off between throughput and resolution. Widefield fluorescence imaging enables large-scale studies but typically requires laborious manual annotation. We investigated whether widefield imaging suffices for reliable mitochondrial morphometry and how few expert annotations are needed for high-content screening. Using 259 images of human umbilical vein endothelial cells spanning FCCP-induced injury and recovery, we assessed inter-annotator reproducibility, four deep learning architectures, training budgets, and image selection strategies. Repeated expert annotations on 40× widefield images showed limited pixel agreement (median Dice, 0.780) but consistent morphometric measurements. U-Net and nnU-Net achieved comparable median test Dice (0.860 and 0.861), and all four architectures broadly preserved morphological distributions. Five training images marked the annotation-efficiency knee point; ten reduced the mean Dice deficit below 0.03, with no detectable differences in selected morphometric measurements versus expert references. The strategy generalized to MRC-5 fibroblasts across fibrosis transition (median Dice, 0.874-0.877 on a 30-image validation set). With only ten annotations, we profiled over 215,000 mitochondrial structures across 254 images, revealing time-dependent remodeling during fibrosis-to-mesenchymal transition and astragaloside IV-associated morphological responses. This approach makes population-scale mitochondrial quantification accessible to routine cell biology laboratories.
